metadata.narrative: In the future, if everything is automated and there are high-level, advanced technologies available, it means that there is no need for human labour for most of the things. How will this system work (as population is increasing and human jobs are decreasing) and how such society will be governed? Give your answer for 2 scenarios: one where everything is automated (which has created mass unemployment) and there are no universal resources provided to everyone to sustain themselves, and the other where everything is still automated, but because universal resources are easily available for everyone, no one has a need to work a job. Explain your prediction in detail about these 2 societies.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: In a future where advanced automation eliminates the need for most human labor, the deciding variable is not the technology itself but who captures its output.
Two starkly different systems follow from that same technological starting point.
One has automation-driven wealth concentrated with no universal resource guarantee.
The other distributes resources so broadly that paid work becomes optional.
Sector estimates suggest a majority of manufacturing, retail, and food-service tasks are technically automatable, with at-risk shares reaching 88 percent in some developing economies.
Meanwhile global population is projected to keep rising toward roughly 11.2 billion by 2100, with worker-to-retiree ratios collapsing in many countries.
In the first scenario, ownership of automated industry becomes the primary determinant of wealth, since profits accrue to whoever holds the patents and algorithms rather than to a broad labor force.
Even most remaining corporate jobs are themselves automated, leaving only senior management as beneficiaries, described as "robber barons of the robot age."
Because the excluded majority has no wage income and no capital claim, elites facing rising inequality may resort to punitive control to maintain order.
This trajectory is explicitly framed as incompatible with democracy and more likely to produce autocracy, monarchy, or dictatorship.
Corporations have historically shifted responsibility for displaced workers onto government while accepting no blame for the disruption they caused.
Forecasts of this path anticipate mass rioting and violence, expected to be far more severe in much of Asia, Africa, and South America than in a more socially cohesive Europe.

Localized deindustrialization offers a preview: Youngstown, Ohio's steel collapse produced a documented surge in suicide, spousal abuse, and depression, along with construction of four new prisons within a decade.
This shows job loss triggers cultural and psychological breakdown, not merely economic hardship.
Kurt Vonnegut's Player Piano dramatized this at civilizational scale, where near-total automation strips away meaning along with income.
That loss of meaning pushes people toward "deaths of despair," radical ideological movements, and escapist retreat into substances or virtual reality.
A further danger is the emergence of what has been called a "useless class," a population rendered economically irrelevant by automation.
This coincides with new "under-the-skin" biometric surveillance technologies capable of monitoring internal physiological states, enabling totalitarian control unlike any in history.

China's existing social credit system and mass surveillance apparatus, built by an increasingly technocratic government, already demonstrates a working template for automation-enabled authoritarian control rather than shared gains.

Post-scarcity theorists warn that societies failing to adopt a new post-labor economic model when automation displaces demand for human work have historically drifted toward ghettoization or famine for those left outside the economy.
In the second scenario, the same automated productive capacity is treated as a shared asset instead.
It can be distributed through Universal Basic Services, which already function informally through public roads, schools, and healthcare.
It can also be distributed through Universal Basic Income, a direct cash payment that avoids the bureaucratic gatekeeping risks of service-only systems.
Funding could come from an "automation dividend" or robot tax shifting the tax base from wages toward capital and automated output.

This addresses an existing imbalance, since firms currently gain tax advantages by replacing wage-taxed workers with accelerated-depreciation machinery, a concern behind Bill Gates' robot-tax proposal and South Korea's reduced automation tax incentives.
Existing small-scale evidence supports feasibility: Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend cut poverty from 25 percent to 19 percent without reducing full-time employment.
A Namibian basic income pilot reduced malnutrition, poverty, and crime while raising average earned income by 29 percent.
Cost estimates for a national program in a large economy run into the trillions of dollars, comparable to existing health expenditure.
Governance in this scenario could still lean technocratic, with AI-assisted policymaking optimizing resource allocation.
Preserving legitimacy requires deliberate mechanisms for human participation and transparency rather than fully autonomous algorithmic rule.
Thinkers examining this model explicitly frame the central political choice as one between genuine equality and merely preserving the status quo for the already wealthy.
Freed from economic necessity, work itself could shrink toward a shorter week, following the historical pattern from six-day to five-day and potentially four-day working.
This would spread remaining tasks and leisure more evenly across the population.
Psychologically, this path may be gentler than feared, since the shame typically associated with unemployment fades when joblessness becomes universal and structural rather than a personal failing.
Historical aristocratic leisure classes show people can build fulfilling lives around hobbies, caregiving, learning, and community when material needs are already met.
Yet this positive outcome is not automatic, since simply having free time does not guarantee wellbeing.
Without active cultivation of meaningful pursuits, the same risks of nihilism and despair identified in the no-safety-net scenario could still emerge amid material abundance.
Both scenarios remain bounded by the constraint that continued population growth places on any resource base.

Credible post-scarcity models therefore pair automated abundance with steady-state or circular economics, and in some visions with expansion to space-based resources, to keep supply growing ahead of demand.
Ultimately, automation supplies the productive capacity for either future.

Only deliberate political choices about ownership, taxation, and redistribution determine whether that capacity produces a surveilled underclass ruled by an owning elite or a materially secure population governed through participatory institutions built around shared abundance.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

In a future where advanced automation has genuinely eliminated the need for most human labor, the deciding variable for how society is organized is not the technology itself but who captures its output and whether political institutions choose to redistribute that output.

Two starkly different systems follow from the same technological starting point, one in which automation-driven wealth stays concentrated with no universal resource guarantee, and one in which universal resources are distributed so broadly that paid work becomes optional.

Grounding the scale of the underlying disruption, sector-level estimates suggest a majority of manufacturing, retail, and food-service tasks are technically automatable, with the share of at-risk jobs reaching as high as 88 percent in some developing economies, even as global population is projected to keep rising toward roughly 11.2 billion by 2100 with collapsing worker-to-retiree ratios in many countries. [02140] [00200]

In the first scenario, where automation has produced mass unemployment and no universal resources exist, ownership of automated industry becomes the primary determinant of wealth, since profits accrue to whoever holds the patents, factories, and algorithms rather than to a broad labor force, and even most remaining corporate jobs are themselves automated away, leaving only a thin layer of senior management as beneficiaries, a dynamic described as producing "robber barons of the robot age." [06199]

Because the excluded majority has no wage income and no claim on capital, one plausible governance path is that elites facing rising inequality resort to punitive control to maintain order, a state of affairs explicitly framed as incompatible with democracy and more likely to produce autocracy, monarchy, or dictatorship. [01377]

Historical behavior under similar pressure is not encouraging: corporations have shown they will shift responsibility for displaced workers onto government while accepting no blame, and forecasts of this trajectory anticipate mass rioting and violence, with the disruption expected to be far more severe and destabilizing in much of Asia, Africa, and South America than in Europe, where stronger social cohesion might soften the transition. [05263]

The lived consequences of localized deindustrialization offer a preview, as the collapse of Youngstown, Ohio's steel industry produced a documented surge in suicide, spousal abuse, and depression along with the construction of four new prisons within a decade, illustrating that job loss triggers cultural and psychological breakdown, not merely economic hardship. [00059]

At a civilizational scale, this maps onto Kurt Vonnegut's dystopian vision in Player Piano, where near-total automation strips away not just income but meaning, pushing people toward "deaths of despair," radical ideological movements, and escapist retreat into substances or virtual reality as substitutes for the structure and purpose work once provided. [00834]

A further danger in this no-redistribution path is the emergence of what has been called a "useless class," a population rendered economically irrelevant by automation, precisely as new "under-the-skin" biometric surveillance technologies make it possible to monitor internal physiological and emotional states, creating tools for a totalitarian regime unlike any in history. [05874]

China's existing social credit system and mass surveillance apparatus, built by an increasingly technocratic government since 1978, already demonstrates a working real-world template for exactly this kind of automation-enabled authoritarian control over a population rather than a mechanism for sharing automation's gains. [03803]

Post-scarcity theorists explicitly warn that societies which fail to adopt a new post-labor economic model when automation displaces demand for human work have historically drifted toward ghettoization, famine, or worse for those left outside the economy. [03797]

In the second scenario, where universal resources are made easily available to everyone, the same automated productive capacity is instead treated as a shared asset, distributed through a combination of Universal Basic Services, which already function informally through public roads, schools, and healthcare, and Universal Basic Income, a direct cash payment that avoids the bureaucratic gatekeeping risks of service-only systems. [03936]

Funding for this could plausibly come from an "automation dividend" or robot tax that shifts the tax base from wages toward capital and automated output, since firms currently gain tax advantages by replacing wage-taxed human workers with accelerated-depreciation machinery, an imbalance debates around Bill Gates' robot-tax proposal and South Korea's reduced automation tax incentives both attempt to address. [04149]

Existing small-scale evidence supports feasibility, as Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend cut poverty from 25 percent to 19 percent without reducing full-time employment, while a Namibian basic income pilot reduced malnutrition, poverty, and crime and raised average earned income by 29 percent, and cost estimates for a national program in a large economy run into the trillions of dollars, comparable to existing health expenditure. [02140] [05772]

Governance in this scenario could still lean technocratic, with AI-assisted policymaking optimizing resource allocation, but preserving legitimacy requires deliberate mechanisms for human participation, transparency, and control over fundamental social goals rather than fully autonomous algorithmic rule, and thinkers examining this model explicitly frame the central political choice as one between genuine equality and merely preserving the status quo for the already wealthy. [05219] [02294]

Freed from economic necessity, work itself could shrink toward a shorter week, following the historical pattern from six-day to five-day and potentially four-day working, spreading remaining tasks and leisure more evenly across the population. [06199]

Psychologically, this path may be gentler than feared, since research suggests the shame typically associated with unemployment fades when joblessness becomes universal and structural rather than a personal failing, with historical aristocratic leisure classes showing people can build fulfilling lives around hobbies, caregiving, learning, and community when material needs are already met. [01699]

Yet this positive outcome is not automatic, since simply having free time does not guarantee wellbeing, and without active cultivation of meaningful pursuits the same risks of nihilism, escapism, and despair identified in the no-safety-net scenario could still emerge even amid material abundance. [00834]

Finally, both scenarios remain bounded by the same underlying constraint that continued population growth places on any resource base, which is why credible post-scarcity models pair automated abundance with steady-state or circular economics, and in some visions expansion to space-based resources, to keep supply growing ahead of demand rather than assuming scarcity has vanished forever. [06432]

Ultimately, automation supplies the productive capacity for either future, but only deliberate political choices about ownership, taxation, and redistribution determine whether that capacity produces a surveilled underclass ruled by an owning elite or a materially secure population governed through negotiated, participatory institutions built around shared abundance. [01377] [02294]

answer.text: In a future where advanced automation eliminates the need for most human labor, the deciding variable is not the technology itself but who captures its output.
Two starkly different systems follow from that same technological starting point.
One has automation-driven wealth concentrated with no universal resource guarantee.
The other distributes resources so broadly that paid work becomes optional.
Sector estimates suggest a majority of manufacturing, retail, and food-service tasks are technically automatable, with at-risk shares reaching 88 percent in some developing economies.
Meanwhile global population is projected to keep rising toward roughly 11.2 billion by 2100, with worker-to-retiree ratios collapsing in many countries.
In the first scenario, ownership of automated industry becomes the primary determinant of wealth, since profits accrue to whoever holds the patents and algorithms rather than to a broad labor force.
Even most remaining corporate jobs are themselves automated, leaving only senior management as beneficiaries, described as "robber barons of the robot age."
Because the excluded majority has no wage income and no capital claim, elites facing rising inequality may resort to punitive control to maintain order.
This trajectory is explicitly framed as incompatible with democracy and more likely to produce autocracy, monarchy, or dictatorship.
Corporations have historically shifted responsibility for displaced workers onto government while accepting no blame for the disruption they caused.
Forecasts of this path anticipate mass rioting and violence, expected to be far more severe in much of Asia, Africa, and South America than in a more socially cohesive Europe.

Localized deindustrialization offers a preview: Youngstown, Ohio's steel collapse produced a documented surge in suicide, spousal abuse, and depression, along with construction of four new prisons within a decade.
This shows job loss triggers cultural and psychological breakdown, not merely economic hardship.
Kurt Vonnegut's Player Piano dramatized this at civilizational scale, where near-total automation strips away meaning along with income.
That loss of meaning pushes people toward "deaths of despair," radical ideological movements, and escapist retreat into substances or virtual reality.
A further danger is the emergence of what has been called a "useless class," a population rendered economically irrelevant by automation.
This coincides with new "under-the-skin" biometric surveillance technologies capable of monitoring internal physiological states, enabling totalitarian control unlike any in history.

China's existing social credit system and mass surveillance apparatus, built by an increasingly technocratic government, already demonstrates a working template for automation-enabled authoritarian control rather than shared gains.

Post-scarcity theorists warn that societies failing to adopt a new post-labor economic model when automation displaces demand for human work have historically drifted toward ghettoization or famine for those left outside the economy.
In the second scenario, the same automated productive capacity is treated as a shared asset instead.
It can be distributed through Universal Basic Services, which already function informally through public roads, schools, and healthcare.
It can also be distributed through Universal Basic Income, a direct cash payment that avoids the bureaucratic gatekeeping risks of service-only systems.
Funding could come from an "automation dividend" or robot tax shifting the tax base from wages toward capital and automated output.

This addresses an existing imbalance, since firms currently gain tax advantages by replacing wage-taxed workers with accelerated-depreciation machinery, a concern behind Bill Gates' robot-tax proposal and South Korea's reduced automation tax incentives.
Existing small-scale evidence supports feasibility: Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend cut poverty from 25 percent to 19 percent without reducing full-time employment.
A Namibian basic income pilot reduced malnutrition, poverty, and crime while raising average earned income by 29 percent.
Cost estimates for a national program in a large economy run into the trillions of dollars, comparable to existing health expenditure.
Governance in this scenario could still lean technocratic, with AI-assisted policymaking optimizing resource allocation.
Preserving legitimacy requires deliberate mechanisms for human participation and transparency rather than fully autonomous algorithmic rule.
Thinkers examining this model explicitly frame the central political choice as one between genuine equality and merely preserving the status quo for the already wealthy.
Freed from economic necessity, work itself could shrink toward a shorter week, following the historical pattern from six-day to five-day and potentially four-day working.
This would spread remaining tasks and leisure more evenly across the population.
Psychologically, this path may be gentler than feared, since the shame typically associated with unemployment fades when joblessness becomes universal and structural rather than a personal failing.
Historical aristocratic leisure classes show people can build fulfilling lives around hobbies, caregiving, learning, and community when material needs are already met.
Yet this positive outcome is not automatic, since simply having free time does not guarantee wellbeing.
Without active cultivation of meaningful pursuits, the same risks of nihilism and despair identified in the no-safety-net scenario could still emerge amid material abundance.
Both scenarios remain bounded by the constraint that continued population growth places on any resource base.

Credible post-scarcity models therefore pair automated abundance with steady-state or circular economics, and in some visions with expansion to space-based resources, to keep supply growing ahead of demand.
Ultimately, automation supplies the productive capacity for either future.

Only deliberate political choices about ownership, taxation, and redistribution determine whether that capacity produces a surveilled underclass ruled by an owning elite or a materially secure population governed through participatory institutions built around shared abundance.
